name: Good psychiatric management (GPM) for borderline personality disorder
evidenceLevel: In a randomized trial of 180 adults with borderline personality disorder (McMain et al., 2009), general psychiatric management led to improvements in suicidal and self-harm episodes, emergency visits and symptoms similar to DBT over one year. John Gunderson later refined it as a generalist model (review: Gunderson and Masland, 2018). NICE CG78 stresses structured, consistent care for borderline personality disorder.
purpose: A practical, generalist approach to borderline personality disorder that clinicians without specialist therapy training can use. It combines honest psychoeducation about the condition and its often good long-term course, a focus on life outside therapy (work, school, relationships), case management, an active and supportive stance, and a shared understanding of interpersonal hypersensitivity: feeling connected is steadying, while feeling rejected or alone can quickly lead to anger, self-harm or dissociation. Medication is used cautiously, mainly for co-occurring conditions.
steps: Discuss the working diagnosis openly (the clinician decides any diagnosis), and explain that many people improve substantially over time.
Introduce the interpersonal hypersensitivity model with the client's own examples: connection, then perceived rejection or threat, then anger or self-harm, then aloneness.
Set expectations: a practical, goal-focused treatment, with life outside treatment, especially work or school, as the main priority.
Take an active, thoughtful, supportive stance: express concern, check your understanding, and admit mistakes.

Make a collaborative safety plan for self-harm and suicidal crises. Respond with concern and practical steps rather than automatic escalation, using your clinical judgment about safety (this app does not assess or decide risk).
Use medication cautiously, as an adjunct, and avoid piling up medicines; coordinate with prescribers.
With consent, involve family through psychoeducation; consider adding a group or specialist therapy if progress stalls over several months.
Review progress against life goals regularly and adjust the plan.
script: Borderline personality disorder is a name for patterns many people recognize. It's treatable, and most people get much better over time.
It sounds like when you felt close to him, things were steadier, and when he didn't text back, it felt like rejection, and things got scary fast.
What would it look like to have a job or a class that gives your week some shape?
Let's make a plan together for what you'll do the next time the urge to hurt yourself comes up.
I may get things wrong sometimes. If I do, I want you to tell me.
contraindications: This app does not assess or decide risk. When self-harm or suicidal thoughts come up, follow your setting's risk-assessment and safety-planning procedures. Keep crisis options visible: 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline (US, call or text), the local emergency number, and findahelpline.com.
GPM is a generalist approach. If there is little progress after several months, or self-harm is frequent or severe, consider a specialist therapy such as DBT or MBT.
Avoid making medication the main treatment, and be cautious with medicines that are dangerous in overdose.
Check for co-occurring conditions (substance use, eating disorders, PTSD, depression) that may need their own treatment.
culturalAdaptations: The label carries strong stigma in some communities. Explain it in plain language focused on patterns and hope, and let the client decide how to talk about it with others.
Interpersonal sensitivity may be heightened by real experiences of rejection, racism or exclusion; acknowledge them.
Work and family roles vary; set 'life outside therapy' goals with the client in their cultural context.
Use a trained professional interpreter rather than family members, and check that key ideas carry the intended meaning in the client's language.
trainingRequired: GPM: designed for generalist clinicians; a short course (for example, through the Gunderson Personality Disorders Institute at McLean Hospital) is recommended before using it as a treatment model.
